This page holds the statistical detail behind the [organizer summary](en.qmd). Every number is read from the simulation outputs when the site is rendered. The model, its assumptions and the sources are on the [Methods](methods.qmd), [Assumptions](assumptions.qmd) and [Literature](literature.qmd) pages.

Two kinds of interval appear. An interval "of the median" is a 95% bootstrap interval for the typical night. A "range across nights" covers 5% to 95% of the simulated nights and shows how different one plausible night is from another.

## What was observed and what matches it

The 2026 observations come from the attendees who ran this study. At 15:30 buying was relatively quick, although it still took a while. Between 18:00 and 20:00 (God Module and Das Ich) the beer exchange line alone took more than 40 minutes for a person who already held tickets, and both the ticket line and the exchange lines were long. After 20:00 they stopped trying to buy, so every wait after that hour is a prediction of the model. The hall was near its fullest around 22:00. One window sold tickets for every drink, two lines exchanged beer and one exchanged cocktails and shots, and people bought several beers per visit for friends.

Waits are reported as the median time until service, estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method. A person who gave up waited at least until leaving the line, and counting that time as a completed wait would understate lines in which many people give up.

The unknown inputs (how many people drink and how fast, patience, group size, people serving beer, time per ticket sale and per beer) were sampled with a sequential approximate Bayesian computation sampler. Of 8\,192 simulated nights in 7 stages, 65 pass every test in the last stage (effective sample size 30). A weighted resample of 64 nights is used for everything below. In those nights 2 to 5 people serve beer, the ticket window takes a median of 29 s per buyer and the first beer of a visit 57 s.

In the matching nights, between 18:00 and 20:00, the ticket line holds 37 people and the beer exchange lines 102. A person who joins an exchange line waits 42 min (range across nights 34 to 69), the ticket window takes 17 min, and a buyer without tickets needs 67 min for the whole purchase (55 to 104). The predicted wait in the exchange line at 21:30 to 22:30 is 79 min (57 to 112). The hall holds 1\,559 people at its fullest (range across nights 1\,291 to 1\,725), and the bar sells 3\,086 beers (2\,134 to 4\,245). The width of that last range is the reason the number of beers sold in 2026 is the first record requested from the organizers.

![](assets/figures/01_calibration_posterior.png){fig-alt="Range tried and matching values for each unknown input"}

The two line tests require at least 20 people in each line. A stricter reading of 30 people keeps about half of the nights. The plan performs as follows in the two groups.

| Nights | Count | Wait of 1 in 10 buyers in 2026 (min) | With the plan (min) | Extra beers with the plan |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| at least 30 in each line | 25 | 93 | 3.0 | +3,530 |
| 20 to 30 in one of the lines | 23 | 83 | 3.3 | +3,255 |


| Outcome, 18:00 to 20:00 | Three inputs with the largest effect, in order |
|:--|:--|
| Wait in the exchange line | serving time\, first beer \(s\); people serving beer; ticket window\, s per buyer |
| People in the ticket line | ticket window\, s per buyer; spare tickets per visit\, plus 1; serving time\, first beer \(s\) |
| People in the exchange lines | serving time\, first beer \(s\); ticket window\, s per buyer; people serving beer |

![](assets/figures/02_calibration_regressions.png){fig-alt="Regression coefficients of the wait and of each line on the unknown inputs"}

![](assets/figures/03_time_series_occupancy_lines.png){fig-alt="People inside the hall and people in each line through the night"}

## Effect of each setup

Every setup reruns the same 48 nights with the same people and the same random seed, so each difference is that night's counterfactual. The plan is payment at the serving station with 10 stations and 9 roaming sellers on the floor from 18:00 to 02:30. The wait of 1 in 10 buyers is taken over everyone who joins a line between 18:00 and 02:00, the hours in which lines formed in 2026.

| Setup | Wait of 1 in 10 buyers, min (interval of the median) | Beers sold (interval of the median) | Nights with a shorter wait (exact 95% lower bound) | Wilcoxon p |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 4 ticket windows | -2.4 (-4.1 to -1.1) | +2 (-13 to +20) | 40 of 48 (at least 70%) | < 0.001 |
| Tickets sold with entry + 5-packs | -2.3 (-3.4 to -0.7) | +32 (+12 to +42) | 34 of 48 (at least 56%) | < 0.001 |
| 2026 setup + 6 roaming sellers | -34.3 (-38.3 to -31.6) | +2,070 (+2,008 to +2,132) | 48 of 48 (at least 93%) | < 0.001 |
| 2026 setup + 2-station satellite bar | -25.6 (-33.2 to -21.6) | +1,112 (+999 to +1,173) | 48 of 48 (at least 93%) | < 0.001 |
| Pay at the station (card/cash), same staff | -7.9 (-11.7 to -5.7) | +322 (+278 to +374) | 46 of 48 (at least 86%) | < 0.001 |
| Cashless wristband at the station, same staff | -14.6 (-18.2 to -11.2) | +552 (+505 to +603) | 48 of 48 (at least 93%) | < 0.001 |
| Cashless stations + 3 extra stations 19:30–01:30 | -41.1 (-48.3 to -36.7) | +1,665 (+1,568 to +1,776) | 48 of 48 (at least 93%) | < 0.001 |
| Wristbands + satellite bar + 4 sellers (2026 staff + 6) | -65.6 (-73.6 to -59.6) | +2,700 (+2,502 to +2,947) | 48 of 48 (at least 93%) | < 0.001 |
| Plan (pay at the station, recommended crew) | -83.8 (-89.6 to -79.8) | +3,265 (+2,904 to +3,521) | 48 of 48 (at least 93%) | < 0.001 |


![](assets/figures/05_counterfactual_effects.png){fig-alt="Effect of each setup on the wait, beers sold and abandoned attempts"}

With the plan the wait of 1 in 10 buyers falls by 83\.8 min (interval of the median 79\.8 to 89\.6) to 3\.1 min, and the bar sells 3\,265 more beers (2\,904 to 3\,521; range across nights 1\,978 to 4\,886). At an assumed MXN 80 per beer that is MXN 261\,200 in sales (232\,355 to 281\,680). Costs of staff and card fees are not in this figure.

![](assets/figures/04_wait_by_time.png){fig-alt="Typical time in line by time of joining for each setup against 2026"}

## The plan against the alternatives

Differences on the same night, second setup minus first, with the 95% interval of the median.

| Comparison | Wait of 1 in 10 buyers | Beers sold | Staff |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Pay at the station with the 2026 head count, then the plan | \-76\.2 min \(\-83\.4 to \-70\.6\) | \+3\,024 \(\+2\,718 to \+3\,197\) | \+15 |
| The plan, then wristbands + satellite bar + 4 sellers | \+21\.4 min \(\+14\.7 to \+24\.3\) | \-432 \(\-578 to \-280\) | \-9 |
| Card or cash at the station, then cashless wristbands | \-4\.8 min \(\-6\.1 to \-4\.2\) | \+237 \(\+216 to \+270\) | \+0 |

Roaming sellers sell 48% of the beers under the plan (range across nights 44% to 53%). A seller carries 6 beers per trip and refills at an end of the bar in 2 min. There were no sellers in 2026, so these rules are assumptions, and the crew without sellers is the fallback.

Payment at the station with the same head count as 2026 leaves a wait of 79\.5 min for 1 in 10 buyers (up to 105\.7 min in the worst 5% of nights).

## Staffing reliability

A night meets the target when 9 of 10 buyers who join a line between 18:00 and 02:00 wait at most 10 min and at most 5% of purchase attempts are abandoned. A crew is recommended when it meets the target in at least 90% of the nights, and among those the one with the fewest staff hours is chosen. For 2\,000 tickets that crew meets the target in 32 of 32 nights (exact 95% lower bound 89%).

![](assets/figures/12_staffing_reliability.png){fig-alt="Share of nights in which each crew meets the waiting target, by ticket level"}

| Tickets | Stations | Sellers | Nights that meet the target | Wait of 1 in 10 buyers, median night / bad night (min) | Staff hours |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1,500 | 6 | 9 | 31 of 32 | 3.0 / 6.5 | 160 |
| 2,000 | 10 | 9 | 32 of 32 | 3.4 / 5.8 | 216 |
| 2,500 | 12 | 9 | 29 of 32 | 3.7 / 8.3 | 244 |


The bad night is the 90th percentile across nights.

## Capacity

The free floor (audience area without vendor strips and tables) is 708 m². At 2\,000 tickets the people standing on it at the fullest moment amount to 1\.89 per m². NFPA 101 caps assembly areas of up to 930 m² at 2\.2 people/m², and the free floor reaches that value near 2\,300 tickets. For larger areas the cap is 1\.54 people/m², which the free floor reaches near 1\,600 tickets. The free floor is below 930 m² and the whole audience area, with vendor strips and tables, is above it. The hall size comes from a satellite image without a scale bar, with an uncertainty near 10% per side. A hall that much smaller or larger reaches the first value at 1\,900 or 2\,800 tickets. That range comes from rescaling the floor area, without new simulations. The licensed capacity is the legal limit.

![](assets/figures/13_capacity.png){fig-alt="People per m² of free floor at the fullest moment against tickets sold"}

With sellers who start at 19:00 the wait of 1 in 10 buyers is 4\.9 min on the median night and 16\.0 min in the worst 5% of nights, against 3\.1 and 6\.2 min for the plan. Demand rises at 18:00, the hour in which the 2026 lines formed, and in that variant the bar serves it alone for one hour.

![](assets/figures/06_heterogeneous_effects.png){fig-alt="Regression of the extra beers under the plan on the unknown inputs"}

## Time-series models

A regression of beers sold per 5 minutes on people inside and a changeover indicator, with AR(1) errors, was fitted on each night from 18:00 to 02:00. In 2026 each extra 100 people inside added 0\.02 beers per 5 minutes and with the plan 3\.82. A bar whose sales do not follow the crowd is at its limit. The event study shows the lines building after each set ends.

![](assets/figures/09_time_series_models.png){fig-alt="Event study of people in lines around the end of a set and AR(1) regression coefficients"}

## Drinking

With faster service the share of attendees who drink 6 beers or more rises from 3\.6% to 22\.2% (range across nights 11\.4% to 29\.4%). Abbott and Abbott (2000) recommend purchase limits and refusing service to intoxicated patrons, and alcohol was the most common arrest reason in the stadium survey of Ammon and Fried (1999).

## Limits of the study

- The calibration rests on the account of the attendees who ran this study. Sales, entries and service times were not measured.
- People walk in straight lines and pass through each other, so the model cannot compare line layouts, barriers or walkways. Those recommendations come from the literature.
- Cocktails and shots, food, restrooms and evacuation are outside the model.
- There were no roaming sellers in 2026, so the seller rules (how far a seller is seen, time per sale, beers per trip, refill time) are assumed.
- The hall size is an estimate from a satellite image.
- Sales in MXN use an assumed price and exclude costs.

## Reproducing the results

The commands below rebuild every output from the configuration files. The steps and their inputs are described on the [Methods](methods.qmd) page.

```bash
uv sync --group site && rv sync && rv activate
./scripts/run_all.sh
```
